text: The DORA metrics tell you how fast and how safely code moves through your pipeline. They say nothing about whether the people generating that code can stand their day-to-day work. A platform can post great DORA numbers while developers quietly hate using it — the golden path works, but step outside it and you're fighting the platform for a week. Nothing about deployment frequency or lead time captures how it felt to get there.

In 2021, researchers from Microsoft Research and GitHub published 'The SPACE of Developer Productivity,' arguing productivity can't be reduced to one number. They proposed five dimensions instead: Satisfaction and well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication and collaboration, and Efficiency and flow. The point isn't to weight all five equally everywhere — it's that no single dimension, especially Activity on its own, tells you anything trustworthy about whether a team is actually doing well.

Satisfaction is the dimension most teams skip, because it feels soft — but it doesn't have to be. A short, recurring pulse survey, run quarterly or monthly, often with an eNPS-style question asking whether someone would recommend the platform to a colleague, turns satisfaction into structured, trackable data. Watch it over time and segmented by team, the same way you'd watch any other metric, instead of treating it as a once-a-year afterthought.

Two more signals are worth collecting directly. Time-to-first-deploy — how long a brand-new engineer takes to ship a real change to production — compresses onboarding docs, local setup, golden path templates, and pipeline reliability into a single number. Cognitive load — how many systems and context switches a developer must juggle for one ordinary change — is harder to reduce to a clean number, but you can count the systems a template touches or simply ask.

Here's the trap: measure developers purely on commit count or pull-request volume, and you'll get more commits and more pull requests — and little else you actually wanted. People optimize for what's measured, not for what you intended. Activity is a legitimate SPACE input alongside Performance and Satisfaction, but dangerous the moment it becomes a target on its own.

DORA and SPACE together cover delivery and experience — but both are still measuring what runs on the platform, or how it feels to use it. Next, we turn the lens on the platform's own services: the CI runner, the GitOps controller, the portal backend. They deserve the same observability rigor as anything they deploy.
